bib.title: ScienceAgentBench: Toward Rigorous Assessment of Language Agents for Data-Driven Scientific Discovery

read.skipped: Reference list and the long code listings in App F/H and licence tables in App J were skimmed, not read line by line.

question: How well do current LLM-based language agents perform individual code-generation tasks drawn from real data-driven scientific discovery workflows?
hypothesis: Agents should be assessed rigorously on individual workflow tasks before claims of end-to-end scientific automation; implied: current agents fall short.
contributions: ScienceAgentBench: 102 tasks from 44 peer-reviewed publications in 4 disciplines, validated by nine subject matter experts
Unified program output with metrics for program, execution result and cost, plus task rubrics
Two strategies against data contamination and agent shortcuts
Evaluation of five LLMs under direct prompting, OpenHands CodeAct and self-debug, plus o1-preview

method.summary: Each task gives an instruction, dataset information and optional expert knowledge; the agent writes a self-contained Python program that is executed in a per-program conda environment and scored by task-specific success criteria. Five LLMs are run under three frameworks, three runs per task, best run kept.
method.task: scientific data-processing, analysis, modelling and visualisation as program generation

datasets.name: ScienceAgentBench
datasets.size: 102 tasks from 44 publications; gold programs average 58.6 lines
datasets.split: all 102 tasks used for evaluation; 110 collected, 106 after dropping 4, 103 after expert review, 102 after annotator verification
datasets.source: open-source code and data of peer-reviewed publications under permissive licences (App J)
datasets.preprocessing: five random test points removed per dataset where possible; model-development tasks re-split with test labels hidden (dummy values such as -1)

other.note: default hyperparameters; only direct prompting and self-debug; reported as reference

other.use: scores figure outputs against ground truth, 3 samples averaged; threshold e.g. >=60

inference.samples: 3 independent runs per task per setting; best run chosen by max SR, then max VER, then max CBS, then min Cost; means and std over 3 runs in Tables E.1/E.2
inference.prompting: 0-shot via API for direct prompting and self-debug; OpenHands has a built-in 1-shot example; with or without expert-provided knowledge; templates in Tables I.1-I.3

parameters.self_debug: re-implemented from Chen et al. 2024a: no reflection step, early exit if same program generated in two consecutive debugging turns, environment built with pipreqs and pip-tools, no basic packages preinstalled
parameters.openhands_codeact: CodeActAgent v1.9 with Python interpreter, bash shell and web browser

other.cost: average USD per task of the selected run (inferred from the best-run selection rule)

metrics.name: Valid Execution Rate (VER)
metrics.definition: program executes without errors and saves output with the correct file name; binary

metrics.name: Success Rate (SR)
metrics.definition: program output meets task-specific executable success criteria; 0 if execution fails; binary

metrics.name: CodeBERTScore (CBS)
metrics.definition: F1 of matched contextual token embeddings against the annotated program; set to 1.0 when SR = 1

metrics.name: API Cost
metrics.definition: average cost to complete one task

metrics.name: Rubric score (human)
metrics.definition: five-stage rubric (Data Loading, Data Processing, Modeling or Visualization, Output formatting, Output Saving), items met summed and normalised to 0-100, averaged over two raters

eval.protocol: Programs run in a conda environment started with numpy, pandas, matplotlib, pytorch, tensorflow, rdkit, tf_keras and extended per program with pipreqs and pip-tools plus hand-written rules. Figures scored by GPT-4o judge (prompt of Yang et al. 2024b, 3 samples averaged). Human rubric evaluation of the 102 programs from the best agent with knowledge, raters not shown execution results. No significance tests.

prompts.text:
You are an expert Python programming assistant that helps scientist users to write high-quality code to solve their tasks.
Given a user request, you are expected to write a complete program that accomplishes the requested task and save any outputs in the correct format.

prompts.purpose: self-debug template (adds: user may execute code and report errors; respond with fixed complete program)
prompts.text:
The user may execute your code and report any exceptions and error messages.
Please address the reported issues and respond with a fixed, complete program.

Then, please run the program to check and fix any errors.
Please do NOT run the program in the background.

limits: Only code-generation capability is tested; other science-agent capabilities (literature, ideas, experiment planning) are out of scope (App A).
Python only, tasks with gold programs under 10 minutes, four disciplines; fewer large-scale or complex tasks (App A).
CodeBERTScore and the GPT-4o figure judge are acknowledged as imperfect; judge-human agreement is not measured here.
Rubric scoring is manual and rubric-derived from the gold program, so valid alternative implementations can be under-rated; no inter-rater agreement reported.
Headline numbers are best-of-3 per task, which flatters agents; means over 3 runs are 5-15 points lower (Tables E.1/E.2).
o1-preview is not compared fairly (different hyperparameters, no OpenHands run).
Contamination mitigations are justified by a single case study (Listing F.4), no quantitative ablation.
No seeds, max turns or step limits stated for self-debug or OpenHands; model results are for 2024 snapshots.
Ablations on knowledge are confounded: tasks where the agent has no idea produce executable but meaningless programs.
